summary: Describes an architecture for sending IP datagrams over MPEG-2 Transport Streams, which are used for digital TV and also as a subnetwork technology. It identifies the need for Internet standards for the interface between the stream and an IP network. It suggests a new encapsulation method and protocols for address resolution and association with logical channels.

eli5.summary: TV broadcast signals can also carry internet data. This memo plans how to pack internet packets inside the TV stream so they come out the other side intact.

subtitle: An architecture for carrying IP over digital TV transport streams, and what is needed to do it well.

tldr.problem: MPEG-2 Transport Streams, used for digital TV and as a subnetwork technology, were designed for audio and video. Existing ways to carry IP over them are not IP-centric and there are no Internet standards for the interface to an IP network.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes the architecture (encapsulator, TS Logical Channels identified by PID, receivers), sets requirements for a new IP-centric encapsulation, and sets requirements for unicast and multicast address resolution that map IP addresses to the multiplex, PID and link address.
tldr.outcome: It is a framework and requirements document, not a protocol. It points to ULE and an address resolution protocol, both still Work in Progress when it was written.

today: RFC 4259 is an Informational framework with no recorded obsoleting or updating RFC. It describes requirements and architecture only, and refers to ULE and an address resolution protocol that were still Work in Progress in its references.

sections.title: IP Over MPEG-2 Networks
sections.content:
RFC 4259 identifies requirements and an architecture for transporting IP datagrams over ISO MPEG-2 Transport Streams (TS). The aim is efficient and flexible delivery of IP services over subnetworks that use the TS, such as those based on Digital Video Broadcast (DVB) and the Advanced Television Systems Committee (ATSC) standards. Such systems typically offer unidirectional (simplex) physical and link layers.

MPEG-2 components are also used to build IP-only networks. The networks may offer link-level broadcast and often need to reach a very large number of nodes. Since most are bandwidth-limited, an encapsulation must add minimal overhead while staying simple, robust to errors and security threats, and extensible.
sections.eli5: The same pipes that carry TV shows can also carry internet data, if you pack the data in carefully.

sections.title: The MPEG-2 Transmission Architecture
sections.content:
An MPEG-2 multiplex carries many parallel TS Logical Channels. Each is identified by a 13-bit Packet ID (PID) in the header of every TS Packet, so values run from 0 to 8191, and 8191 (0x1FFF) marks a null packet that keeps the bit rate constant. A TS Packet is a fixed 188 bytes with a 4-byte header. Unlike an ATM virtual channel, a PID is a unidirectional broadcast channel rather than a point-to-point link, and there is no standard interface to set up connections or map IP flows or QoS to PIDs.

The memo describes six scenarios: broadcast TV and radio, broadcast networks used as an ISP, a unidirectional star IP network, a datacast overlay, point-to-point links and two-way IP networks. Only the first two mainly carry video and audio for set-top boxes. A re-multiplexor may renumber PIDs to avoid clashes.

To send IP, an Encapsulator turns each protocol data unit (PDU) such as an IP packet or Ethernet frame into a Sub-Network Data Unit (SNDU) by adding a header and trailer, then fragments it into TS Packets. A Receiver filters the PIDs it wants and reassembles each SNDU independently. Packets of one IP flow must use the same PID, and many hardware filters limit the active PIDs (for example 32).
sections.eli5: The stream is like a big pipe split into numbered lanes. Internet packets are cut up, sent down a lane, and glued back together at the other end.

sections.title: Requirements for a New Encapsulation
sections.content:
Existing options include ATM AAL5 and DVB Multi-Protocol Encapsulation (MPE). The memo says MPE has optional header parts and requires decoding control headers, which costs receiver processing and some link overhead for Internet traffic, and that IPv6, MPLS and other network protocols are not natively supported. This justifies a new, truly IP-centric encapsulation.

The requirements it lists are:

  • Payload unit delimitation using the PUSI bit, with the ability to pack more than one SNDU into a TS Packet and to tell padding from a following SNDU.
  • A Length Indicator in the header, supporting at least the Ethernet MTU of 1500 bytes; 16 KB is suggested as a suitable maximum.
  • A Next Level Protocol Type field covering at least IPv4 and IPv6, and leaving room for other values such as ROHC or bridging.
  • An optional Network Point of Attachment (NPA) address, since NPA filtering is only weak security.
  • A strong integrity check, a CRC in a trailer; a CRC-32 is described as sufficient for up to a 12 KB payload.
  • Extension headers, so new features need no out-of-band configuration.

The summary adds low or managed overhead, easy hardware or software implementation, compatibility with legacy deployments and support for link encryption.
sections.eli5: The wrapping paper should say how long the parcel is, what is inside, and have a seal that shows if it got damaged, all without being heavy.

sections.title: Address Resolution
sections.content:
Address resolution (AR) links layer 2 information to an IP address. For MPEG-2 a Receiver needs three things: a Receiver ID such as a 6-byte MAC/NPA address, a PID or an index to find one, and tuner information such as the transmit frequency. PIDs are not intended to be end-to-end identifiers, so re-multiplexors can make the indirection necessary.

AR information could be sent in three ways: in MPEG-2 signalling tables at the MPEG-2 level, in tables sent over IP (the memo says no implementations are known), or through a query/response protocol over IP in the style of IPv6 Neighbor Discovery, which has good soft-state properties and tolerates failures.

The memo also requires scoping: private IPv4 prefixes such as 10/8, 172.16/12 and 192.168/16, and NPA addresses, must not leak into other addressed areas. Leaks give a possible denial of service and, when the Receiver is a router, arbitrary packets reaching the IP layer. AR also needs authentication, since wireless links let unauthorized hosts claim L2 resources.

The unicast requirements are a table-based approach for scaling, a way to install and verify information at the server, a way to purge client information, subnetwork scoping and security associations to authenticate the sender.
sections.eli5: A receiver needs a phone book that says which lane and which address to listen to for each internet address, and it should only trust a phone book from a source it can verify.

sections.title: Multicast Support
sections.content:
The primary goal is efficient filtering of IP multicast at the Receiver and mapping IPv4 and IPv6 multicast addresses to a PID and TS Multiplex. The design should permit a large number of active groups and keep receiver processing low, with schemes that are easy to do in hardware.

Receivers normally learn group membership with IGMP for IPv4 or MLD for IPv6, or a multicast routing protocol, and in the dynamic case that membership is fed back to the sender so it can start new groups and update its AR tables. AR should associate a PID with a group address and possibly a QoS class, and explicit per-group AR to individual L2 addresses is to be avoided.

Scoped multicast ranges, such as 224.0.0/24, 224.0.1/24 and the 239/8 administratively scoped range, must stay in their area. The multicast requirements are encapsulating multicast, mapping groups to PID and multiplex, giving AR information so receivers can find a flow, and error reporting.
sections.eli5: For group broadcasts, the receiver tells the sender which shows it wants, and the sender puts each show on its own lane.

sections.title: Security and Link Encryption
sections.content:
The memo says end-to-end security such as TLS, PGP and S/MIME, SSH or IPsec is recommended on any path, especially one with a wireless or broadcast link. Subnetwork security is still valuable because users of shared or radio networks often control at most one endpoint, and it can protect against traffic analysis and attacks on control functions such as address resolution.

Encrypting at the Transport Stream level scrambles the whole SNDU including the NPA address, which forces a Receiver to decrypt everything before filtering, and all Receivers must share a key. MPE supports optional link encryption indicated by a pair of header bits. The memo recommends that any new IETF encapsulation allow TS encryption and optional link-level encryption or authentication of the payload; in ULE this could be done with Extension Headers.

It has no IANA actions of its own, though protocols meeting the requirements will need assignments.
sections.eli5: Locks work best on the parcel itself, but a lock on the whole mail truck helps too, so both can be used.
